acc-aha:cir-0000000000000613.summary: This 2018 AHA focused update to the ACLS guidelines reviews evidence on antiarrhythmic drugs given during and immediately after shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation/pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VF/pVT) cardiac arrest. Its key revised recommendation is that providers may consider either amiodarone or lidocaine for shock-refractory VF/pVT.
key_points: For shock-refractory VF/pVT cardiac arrest, either amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered. This is the update's revised recommendation.
The abstract states it is unclear whether antiarrhythmic drugs given during or immediately after VF/pVT arrest improve patient outcomes.
The update covers antiarrhythmic use both during the arrest and in the immediate post-arrest period. The abstract does not give its specific post-arrest recommendations.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000613.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract gives no doses, recommendation class or level of evidence, and no recommendations on post-arrest prophylaxis or other agents (e.g., magnesium, beta-blockers). The population is inferred as adult because this is an ACLS update; the abstract does not state it.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001181.summary: This 2023 AHA/AAP focused update to the neonatal resuscitation guidelines draws on 4 ILCOR Neonatal Life Support Task Force systematic reviews. It covers umbilical cord management in preterm, late preterm, and term newborns, and the devices and interfaces used to give positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) during newborn resuscitation. The abstract says there is new guidance on intact umbilical cord milking, on PPV device selection, and on an additional primary PPV interface, but it does not give the recommendations themselves.
key_points: The update gives new guidance on intact umbilical cord milking, but the abstract does not state which gestational ages it applies to or how strong the recommendation is.
Umbilical cord management was reviewed separately for preterm, late preterm, and term newborns, so cord recommendations may differ by gestational age.
The update addresses which device to choose for delivering PPV during newborn resuscitation; the abstract does not name the preferred device.
An additional primary interface for delivering PPV is now recommended; the abstract does not name it.
The recommendations rest on 4 ILCOR Neonatal Life Support Task Force systematic reviews and update, rather than replace, the existing AHA CPR and ECC neonatal guidelines.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 AHA Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (neonatal resuscitation)
ILCOR Neonatal Life Support Task Force systematic reviews
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001181.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific recommendations, their strength or class and level of evidence, the gestational-age thresholds for cord milking, and the named PPV devices and interfaces are not provided.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000000732.summary: This 2019 AHA focused update to the ACLS guidelines reviews evidence published since 2015 on three interventions during cardiac arrest: advanced airway strategy (bag-mask ventilation, supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation), vasopressors (standard-dose epinephrine) and extracorporeal CPR. Only the abstract is available. It restates that high-quality CPR plus rapid defibrillation, when appropriate, remain the foundation of resuscitation, but the abstract does not give the specific revised recommendations.
key_points: High-quality CPR combined with rapid defibrillation (when appropriate) remains the foundation of resuscitation; other interventions build on it.
The update revises recommendations on choosing an airway strategy during arrest: bag-mask ventilation, supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation.
It also addresses the initial training and ongoing retraining needed for advanced airway management.
It contains revised recommendations on giving standard-dose epinephrine during cardiac arrest.
It covers decisions about when to use extracorporeal CPR (ECPR) and its possible effect on survival.
The abstract does not give the specific recommendations, their strength (Class/LOE), doses or timing; consult the full text.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000732.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The specific recommendations, classes of recommendation, levels of evidence, doses and ECPR selection criteria are not included. The adult population is inferred from the ACLS scope.

aliem:68055.summary: ALiEM blog summary of the toxicology-specific medication recommendations in the 2020 AHA ACLS guidelines, which mostly apply to poisoned adults in cardiac arrest or refractory shock. The post notes these are fairly basic recommendations. Key takeaways: avoid flumazenil in undifferentiated coma, and use sodium bicarbonate for sodium channel blocker toxicity with cardiac arrest or QRS >120 msec.
key_points: Do not give flumazenil for undifferentiated coma (COR 3, LOE B-R).

For sodium channel blocker toxicity (e.g., TCAs) with cardiac arrest or life-threatening conduction delay such as QRS >120 msec, sodium bicarbonate can be beneficial (COR 2a, LOE C-LD). ECMO may be considered for arrest or refractory shock (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).

Beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker toxicity: high-dose insulin is reasonable for both (2a/C-LD). IV glucagon is reasonable for beta-blockers (2a) and may be considered for CCBs (2b). Calcium is reasonable for CCBs (2a) and may be considered for beta-blockers (2b). ECMO might be considered for either (2b).

Cocaine toxicity with hypertension, tachycardia, agitation or chest discomfort: benzodiazepines, alpha blockers, CCBs, nitroglycerin and/or morphine can be beneficial (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). Avoiding pure beta-blockers may be reasonable, though evidence is contradictory (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).

Other antidotes and therapies: IV lipid emulsion may be reasonable for local anesthetic toxicity (2b, C-LD). Give antidigoxin Fab for severe digoxin toxicity (2b, B-R). Hyperbaric oxygen may help in severe CO poisoning (2b, B-R). Hydroxocobalamin with oxygen, with or without sodium thiosulfate, can be beneficial for cyanide (2a, C-LD).
discusses_guidelines: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support)
aliem:68055.limitations: Brief list-style summary of guideline recommendations. It gives no doses, evidence discussion or caveats beyond the stated COR/LOE, and the recommendations focus mainly on cardiac arrest or refractory shock.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000001194.summary: This 2023 AHA focused update to the adult ACLS guidelines covers new evidence and recommendations on medications, temperature management, coronary angiography, extracorporeal CPR (ECPR), and seizure management in adult cardiac arrest. Only the abstract is available, and it names these topic areas without giving any specific recommendations, doses, or evidence classes.
key_points: The update covers five areas of adult cardiac arrest care: medications, temperature management, percutaneous coronary angiography, ECPR, and seizure management.
The abstract gives no specific recommendations, doses, thresholds, or recommendation classes; consult the full guideline before applying it in practice.
The authors note that recent cardiac arrest research lacks the data needed to evaluate diversity, equity, and inclusion in this population.
The update describes cardiac arrest patients as a potentially important pool of organ donors for people awaiting transplantation.
According to the abstract, cardiac arrest affects up to 700,000 people in the United States each year.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000001194.limitations: Abstract only; full text not available. The abstract lists topics but gives no specific recommendations, doses, temperature targets, ECPR or angiography criteria, or recommendation strength/LOE.

aliem:67992.summary: This ALiEM post (part 1 of 3) summarizes the 2020 AHA ACLS guideline recommendations on vasopressor and non-vasopressor medications during adult cardiac arrest. Its bottom line is that there were no major changes: epinephrine remains recommended (1 mg every 3-5 minutes), given early in non-shockable rhythms and after failed defibrillation in shockable rhythms.
key_points: Epinephrine is recommended in cardiac arrest (COR 1, LOE B-R); 1 mg every 3-5 minutes is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-R).
In non-shockable rhythms, give epinephrine as soon as feasible (COR 2a, LOE C-LD); in shockable rhythms, it may be reasonable after initial defibrillation attempts fail (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
Amiodarone or lidocaine may be considered for VF/pulseless VT unresponsive to defibrillation (COR 2b, LOE B-R).
Vasopressin offers no advantage over epinephrine (COR 2b, LOE C-LD), and steroids during CPR for OHCA are of uncertain benefit (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
Routine calcium (COR 3, LOE B-NR), sodium bicarbonate (COR 3), and magnesium (LOE B-R) are not recommended during cardiac arrest.
discusses_guidelines: 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC, Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support
aliem:67992.limitations: Brief tabular summary of guideline recommendations without discussion of underlying evidence; some LOE/COR entries incomplete (e.g., sodium bicarbonate lacks LOE, magnesium lacks COR). Arrhythmia and toxicology content deferred to later posts.

acc-aha:cir-0000000000000736.summary: This 2019 AHA focused update to pediatric basic life support guidelines addresses dispatcher-assisted CPR (DA-CPR) for infants and children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, based on an ILCOR Pediatric Task Force systematic review of four new pediatric studies. The key takeaway is that emergency medical dispatch centers should offer DA-CPR for presumed pediatric cardiac arrest, especially when no bystander CPR is in progress.
key_points: Emergency medical dispatch centers should offer dispatcher-assisted CPR instructions for presumed pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
DA-CPR is especially recommended when no bystander CPR is already in progress.
DA-CPR was associated with significantly higher rates of bystander CPR and improved survival at 1 month after pediatric cardiac arrest.
No recommendation could be made for or against giving DA-CPR instructions when bystander CPR is already underway.
The evidence base consisted of four new pediatric studies analyzed by the ILCOR Pediatric Task Force as part of its continuous evidence review process.
acc-aha:cir-0000000000000736.limitations: Only the abstract was available; recommendation class and level of evidence, specific effect sizes, and details of the DA-CPR protocol were not provided. The update is narrow in scope, addressing only dispatcher-assisted CPR for pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, and is based on observational association data from four studies.

aliem:68007.summary: This ALiEM post tabulates the 2020 AHA ACLS medication recommendations, with class of recommendation and level of evidence, for adult wide-complex tachycardia, regular narrow-complex tachycardia, atrial fibrillation/flutter with rapid ventricular rate, and bradycardia. The main takeaway is the list of medications flagged as harmful: verapamil in wide-complex tachycardia, and AV nodal blockers or amiodarone in preexcited AF.
key_points: Avoid verapamil in wide-complex tachycardia (COR 3: harm, LOE B-NR). For stable WCT, adenosine may be considered (COR 2b, LOE B-NR), as may amiodarone, procainamide or sotalol (COR 2b, LOE B-R).

In AF/flutter with preexcitation, avoid digoxin, non-dihydropyridine CCBs, beta-blockers and amiodarone (COR 3, LOE C-LD). With LV systolic dysfunction and decompensated HF, avoid non-DHP CCBs and beta-blockers (COR 3, LOE C-EO).
For AF/flutter with rapid ventricular rate, use a beta-blocker, diltiazem or verapamil first (COR 1, LOE B-NR); amiodarone is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-NR).
For regular narrow-complex tachycardia, start with vagal maneuvers and adenosine (both COR 1, LOE B-R). Next options are diltiazem or verapamil (COR 2a, LOE B-R) or beta-blockers (COR 2a, LOE C-LD).
For polymorphic VT with long QT (torsades), give magnesium (COR 2b, LOE C-LD). For polymorphic VT without long QT, consider lidocaine or amiodarone (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).

In bradycardia, treat reversible causes (COR 1, LOE C-EO) and give atropine for hemodynamic compromise (COR 2a, LOE B-NR). If atropine fails, use epinephrine or transcutaneous pacing (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
discusses_guidelines: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC, Part 3: Adult Basic and Advanced Life Support
aliem:68007.limitations: The post is a brief table summary of the guideline. It gives no doses, no criteria for electrical cardioversion or instability, and no supporting evidence discussion.

aliem:74329.summary: ALiEM blog post offering 11 practical pearls plus a charting bonus tip for ED management of epistaxis in adults and children. The authors stress that adults presenting with epistaxis rarely warrant doing "nothing", because bleeding often recurs even when it has stopped. The key technique points are clot evacuation, sustained firm pressure with a topical vasoconstrictor, and tight packing.
key_points: Have the patient blow the nose firmly to clear clots. Spray a vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline if available, then hold firm pressure with a clip or clamp for at least 15 minutes while you gather supplies.
Pack topical vasoconstrictor/anesthetic tightly (cotton, pledgets, swabs) so it contacts the mucosa and tamponades bleeding. Packing both nares may be needed because the septum is mobile.
Acute BP treatment is generally not needed. A calm, confident approach and explaining the procedure often lower BP enough.
For silver nitrate cautery: dry and anesthetize the site first. Roll gently over an area slightly wider than the bleeding site and limit repeat attempts.

For commercial packing: trim oversized tampons at an angle and coat them with antibiotic ointment as a lubricant. Insert along the contour of the nasal passage, then wet with 1-3 mL of water or saline (needleless syringe) to expand and soften.
Observe 15-30 minutes or longer after the procedure before discharge. Confirm hemostasis, packing tolerance and stable vital signs.
Call for help early for: hemodynamic compromise, hypoxia or cardiopulmonary distress, post-surgical bleeding, bleeding tumors (especially irradiated), bleeding disorders, or uncontrolled bleeding.
aliem:74329.limitations: Expert-opinion practical tips with no cited evidence beyond a recommended review article (Gottlieb & Long, Ann Emerg Med 2023). No specific drug doses beyond saline volume, no guidance on anticoagulated patients, and limited pediatric-specific detail.
